title: Anchoring trust in money: innovation beyond stablecoins (Annual Economic Report 2026, Chapter III) — press release
key_claim: Current stablecoin designs fall short on key properties of money, in particular 'singleness' (redemption at par with central bank money); the path forward is to bring tokenisation into the existing two-tier system where central banks provide the anchor and commercial banks provide services, via a 'unified ledger' that integrates tokenised commercial bank deposits and tokenised central bank reserves (as prototyped in Project Agora, 8 central banks and 40+ regulated institutions).
frame_summary: The BIS argues stablecoins are not sound money and that the future monetary system should route tokenisation through the two-tier bank/central-bank structure rather than around it.
notes: Tier-1 multilateral framing. Full AER 2026 published 28 June; this press release (23 June) carries the substantive argument and Project Agora detail.

publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
title: Stablecoins vs. Tokenized Deposits: The Narrow Banking Debate Revisited (Staff Report No. 1179)
date_evidence: 'Number 1179  February 2026 Revised February 2026' ; suggested citation 'Huang, Xuesong, and Todd Keister. 2026. ... no. 1179, February.'
key_claim: In a formal model, if regulatory costs on banks are large and risk-shifting is limited, allowing only tokenized deposits (not stablecoins) in on-chain trade raises welfare by expanding bank credit; if regulation is light and risk-shifting strong, stablecoins-only is preferable; in between, competition is optimal — the tradeoffs mirror historical narrow-banking debates.
frame_summary: The NY Fed models the stablecoin-vs-tokenized-deposit choice as a narrow-banking problem and shows tokenized deposits are welfare-superior wherever bank credit creation matters and risk-shifting is contained.
notes: Structural anchor (Feb 2026): canonical analytical framing for why tokenized deposits, not stablecoins, are the credit-preserving on-chain money. Month-level date; within 180-day audit window.

title: GENIUS Act Requirements and Standards for FDIC-Supervised Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers and Insured Depository Institutions (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking)
date_evidence: WebSearch result: 'Federal Register/Vol. 91, No. 69/Friday, April 10, 2026' ; document number 2026-06974; FDIC Board approved 7 April 2026; comments due 9 June 2026
key_claim: The FDIC's proposed rule provides that a tokenized product meeting the statutory definition of 'deposit' is a deposit — insured under the FDI Act no differently from non-tokenized deposits — while deposits held as reserves backing a payment stablecoin are NOT insured to stablecoin holders on a pass-through basis (they are treated as deposits of the issuer, insured up to $250,000 with respect to the issuer, not each holder).
frame_summary: The FDIC rulemaking hard-codes a regulatory perimeter that keeps the deposit-insurance safety net for tokenized deposits and explicitly denies pass-through insurance to stablecoins.
notes: Tier-1 primary rulemaking. Federal Register page is JS-heavy/large; date taken from FR citation in WebSearch snippet and confirmed by URL path /2026/04/10/. verbatim_quote left null to avoid provenance dependence on a large page.

title: What are the differences between payment stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits?
date_evidence: Visible byline under author Nellie Liang: 'April 14, 2026'
key_claim: Tokenized bank deposits are backed by deposit insurance (to $250,000), the issuing bank's capital and Fed lender-of-last-resort access, and operate within existing banking law; US stablecoins were ~$280bn at year-end 2025 (Tether ~$190bn, Circle ~$80bn) with ~$1.2tn monthly transaction volume; interbank settlement of tokenized deposits on private blockchains 'does not exist'; community banks have less capacity to issue stablecoins or tokenized deposits; US commercial banks hold ~$19tn of deposits.
frame_summary: Brookings' Liang explains that tokenized deposits keep the full bank safety net while stablecoins do not, and flags that interbank interoperability of tokenized deposits is the missing piece and community banks the most exposed.
notes: Tier-2 institutional explainer by a former Fed/Treasury official; source of the quantification anchors on stablecoin scale, the 'interbank settlement does not exist' point, and the community-bank exposure.

publisher: Oxford Business Law Blog (University of Oxford, Faculty of Law)
title: The Contest Between Central Bank Digital Currencies, Stablecoins and Tokenised Deposits: Which Will Likely Win, and Why?
date_evidence: 'Posted: 26 March 2026' ; Author 'Ross P Buckley, ARC Laureate Fellow & Scientia Professor, UNSW Sydney'
key_claim: In the contest to underpin next-generation (especially cross-border) payments, CBDCs are the slow 'tortoise' and stablecoins the fast 'hare', but tokenised bank deposits are a third contender — the 'rhino' — that combines stablecoin-like programmability with prudential regulation, deposit insurance, central-bank liquidity in stress and the ability to pay interest, and will likely prove the most durable model.
frame_summary: Buckley argues tokenised deposits will most likely win the digital-money race because they carry the banking system's prudential and correspondent-banking foundations, which stablecoins lack.
notes: Tier-2 academic (Oxford Law blog summarising the author's Capital Markets Law Journal article, Vol 21 Issue 2, 2026). Correspondent-banking framing anchors the on-chain-hierarchy thesis. Body paraphrases; no verbatim quote used.

title: The Clearing House to launch tokenized deposits system for banks
key_claim: A group of the largest US banks announced on 5 June 2026 that The Clearing House will operate a shared network for clearing and settling tokenized deposits between banks, with a connectivity layer linking on-chain activity to the RTP and CHIPS fiat rails and supporting programmable treasury, 24/7 settlement and agentic-commerce use cases.
frame_summary: The ABA/Clearing House announcement establishes the money-centre banks' shared tokenized-deposit network bridged to the incumbent CHIPS/RTP rails.
notes: Tier-3 trade press (ABA). Primary announcement of the money-centre consortium; JPMorgan/Citi/BofA/Wells + 13 more per the underlying Clearing House statement.

title: Tokenized Deposits Set Up Banking's Next Network Race
key_claim: The Clearing House tokenized-deposit network (JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo and others) is targeted for launch in the first half of 2027; the rollout is likely to echo the RTP-then-FedNow divide, where large institutions build first (RTP, 2017) and smaller institutions gain access later (FedNow, 2023), with technology providers such as FIS (Lyriq) extending tokenized-deposit capability to the rest of the market.
frame_summary: PYMNTS frames tokenized deposits as banking's next network race and predicts a large-bank-first, regional/community-bank-later access divide reminiscent of real-time payments.
notes: Tier-3 trade press. Source for the H1-2027 timeline and the explicit RTP/FedNow tiering analogy that anchors the access-risk thesis; also supplies the coexistence counter-frame (Webster).

title: Regional Banks Team Up for Tokenized Deposits
date_evidence: Visible dateline '02/23/2026 - 09:09' (23 February 2026) ; og:image cache token t=20260223
key_claim: Five regional US banks (Huntington, First Horizon, M&T, KeyCorp, Old National) are building a tokenized-deposit network with the Cari Network (led by former Comptroller Gene Ludwig): MVP in March, pilot in Q3, full commercial rollout by year-end 2026; tokens are FDIC-insured bank liabilities, and the platform will initially support money movement only among the participating banks' own customers, with interoperability with other networks planned later.
frame_summary: Banking Exchange reports mid-size banks banding together in a shared tokenized-deposit consortium to keep insured deposits competitive without each building its own coin.
notes: Tier-3 trade press. Source for the regional Cari consortium specifics and the 'initially only among participating banks' customers' cash-island detail. Body paraphrases; no verbatim quote used.
